Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-21

Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Devin Chu (Lynx CTO), Maya Singh (Infra Lead), Carlos Reyes (ML Eng)

Auto-generated summary: see metadata above.

[00:00] Ava Martinez: hey everybody, thanks for joining. quick intro: i'm ava, i'm the ae on the account, and samir is our systems eng, he'll handle the runtime/perf stuff. devin, maya, carlos, thanks for making time. goal today is to dig into your p95/p99 issues and map to experiments.

[00:22] Devin Chu: yeah thanks. our main pain right now is that under production traffic, p95 is okay-ish, but p99 spikes a lot when models hit longer contexts or when we have bursty requests. hoping to understand whether that's kv cache, batching, or network hops to the private cluster.

[00:45] Samir Patel: cool. can you remind us of the stack? you're running a vpc deployment with some on-prem connect, and using our hosted models initially?

[00:57] Maya Singh: correct — hybrid. most inference runs on Dedicated in our VPC but we have some failover to hosted. models are a 13B open model we fine-tuned. network path is client -> company app -> internal router -> VPC peered cluster -> redwood nodes. sometimes we also have an on-prem gateway that adds an extra hop.

[01:20] Ava Martinez: perfect. objectives: measure p95/p99 with streaming and non-streaming; quantify impact of kv cache hit rate; test batching thresholds (batch sizes and max wait); and evaluate quantized vs full precision latency variance.

[01:45] Samir Patel: i'm going to sketch out the hypothesis first. most of the time tail is caused by three things: cache misses that force full autoregressive decode (so extra kv loads), large dynamic batching leading to head-of-line blocking, and network variability on multi-hop topologies — especially when peering + on-prem firewalls add jitter. quantization usually reduces median latency but can increase variance if kernels fall back to slower paths.

[02:20] Carlos Reyes: interesting — we did see weird outliers when q4_0 was enabled, thought quant helped; but the p99 got worse on some runs.

[02:32] Samir Patel: yep that's consistent. q4_0 reduces compute per token, but some operators for certain attention patterns may hit suboptimal kernels. plus if KV cache misses are high you pay full cost every call which amplifies variance.

[03:00] Ava Martinez: let's go through measurement approach. we recommend synthetic benchmarks with three traffic shapes: steady low qps, bursty fanout, and long-context few-shot pings. measure two modes: streaming (chunked token proto) and non-streaming (full payload). compare p50/p95/p99 and CPU/GPU utilization.

[03:35] Devin Chu: what's the difference in end-to-end for streaming vs non-streaming? we assumed streaming always wins for p99.

[03:44] Samir Patel: streaming helps user-perceived latency because you get tokens earlier, but tail can still be high if initial latency (model startup, KV fetch) is large. non-streaming hides partial tokens but can have higher overall end-to-end since you wait for completion. also, streaming exposes more network chattiness — more round trips if the app is acking small chunks, which can actually amplify network jitter on high-hop topologies.

[04:18] Maya Singh: so in our infra, that extra round-trip is over the peered link and sometimes through an on-prem gateway — that could explain the big p99 spikes.

[04:30] Samir Patel: exactly. the rule of thumb: streaming reduces TTF (time-to-first-token) but doesn't guarantee lower p99 unless you address KV misses and network jitter.

[04:50] Ava Martinez: quick note on metrics collection: we'll want both service-side histograms at the token and request level, plus network traces (tcpdump/pcap or flow logs) for the peering hop. We've seen cases where a 5-10ms tail from the firewall aggregated with 20-30ms variance at the model node creates outsized p99.

[05:20] [timestamped demo doc link shared: /redwood/benchmarks/lynx-2026-04-21-config.xlsx]

[05:38] Samir Patel: let's talk KV caching. what's your observed cache hit rate?

[05:44] Carlos Reyes: in canary it's ~72% but in production around 45% because we have lots of unique user prompts and only prefix-level caching enabled.

[05:54] Samir Patel: 45% is rough. each miss forces a longer decode and adds durable latency. we can try increasing prefix normalization (strip session noise) and moving to per-conversation cache keys to boost hits. also warm cache on deployment/rolling restarts.

[06:18] Devin Chu: are there storage IOPS or network fetchs involved for large kv stores? we host kv cache in-memory on the node?

[06:26] Samir Patel: Redwood's runtime keeps KV cache in-GPU memory for hot prefixes; if it's large we spill to host memory and potentially to a distributed KV store if configured. those extra hops are bad for p99. for Dedicated, we can pin working sets to GPU and tune eviction windows.

[06:48] Maya Singh: sounds like we need to audit our working set footprints. we do have a few long-context threads that rho up the cache.

[07:00] Ava Martinez: let's put a concrete experiment: run a 1k-request benchmark with three configs: 1) streaming + KV on (current prod), 2) streaming + KV warmed with higher hit rate, 3) non-streaming + same. measure p50/p95/p99 and GPU util. Samir will run; devin will share prompts.

[07:25] Samir Patel: on batching: dynamic batching is great for throughput but introduces tail cliffs. our runtime supports two knobs: max_batch_size and max_wait_ms. raising max_wait gives better throughput but longer worst-case wait. for p99-sensitive apps, we often cap max_wait at 10-15ms and keep max_batch moderate.

[07:52] Carlos Reyes: do you have heuristics to auto-adjust based on QPS?

[07:58] Samir Patel: yes, we have adaptive batching that lowers wait when queue latency climbs. but adaptation itself has hysteresis; sudden bursts can still form big batches. for predictable p99 you can set conservative static thresholds or use our routing policy to route a percentage of critical traffic to lower-batch nodes.

[08:25] Devin Chu: explain routing policy?

[08:29] Ava Martinez: we can tag routes by SLO; critical routes go to low-latency pools (smaller batches, prewarmed cache), and best-effort routes go to high-throughput pools. this increases cost a bit but gives predictable p99.

[08:45] Maya Singh: on quantization — we tested q4_0 and q8 on a few models. q8 gave stable improvements, q4_0 had occasional regressions. any mitigations?

[08:56] Samir Patel: mitigations include kernel selection tuning and fallback detection. we instrument to detect when q4_0 kernels hit slow paths and can fallback to q8 for those cases or roll forward a software patch. Also model-specific calibration helps. we'll need to run profile traces to see which ops are causing slowdowns.

[09:24] Ava Martinez: can you share examples of numbers? like median vs p99 for q8 vs fp16?

[09:30] Samir Patel: rough numbers from a similar 13B workload: fp16 median 120ms, p99 420ms. q8 median 95ms, p99 460ms in one env due to kernel mismatch. q4_0 median 75ms, p99 700ms in the worst case — but those p99s are avoidable with kernel tuning and selective fallback.

[10:00] Carlos Reyes: that's quite a delta. probably explains our observed spikes.

[10:08] Ava Martinez: next, network hops. maya you mentioned a gateway; can you describe firewall rules and whether NAT/masquerade is in path?

[10:18] Maya Singh: yes, traffic to the on-prem gateway goes through a NAT device, then palo alto firewall, then into our private datacenter. average added latency ~12ms but we see occasional 100-200ms spikes from firewall DPI.

[10:35] Samir Patel: DPI or threat inspection can be very spiky. for p99 sensitive flows we recommend bypass rules for known egress to Redwood endpoints or a dedicated peering with limited inspection. also TCP connection churn matters—reusing connections and keepalives reduce handshake tails.

[10:58] Devin Chu: hmm we don't have a dedicated route. that may be our biggest offender.

[11:05] Ava Martinez: if you can share firewall logs for the periods of p99 spikes, we can correlate. also we'll instrument flow logs on our side to map RTT and jitter per hop.

[11:20] Samir Patel: also consider TLS termination points. if TLS is terminated at the on-prem gateway then re-encrypted, you get extra CPU jitter. pushing TLS termination closer to the model nodes or using hardware offload helps.

[11:40] Carlos Reyes: for our security folks that's tricky but we can explore exceptions for service-to-service traffic.

[11:50] [15:00] short silence / crosstalk

[12:05] Samir Patel: switching to instrumentation — recommend token-level logs with sampling (1 in 100) plus full traces for outliers. the runtime emits per-token timings, kernel timing, and batching wait. that'll let us attribute a p99 to KV miss vs batch wait vs kernel fallback.

[12:32] Devin Chu: can you show an example trace?

[12:35] Samir Patel: yeah pulling one up... (paraphrase) Trace: request id X: queue_wait 12ms, batch_assembly 6ms, kernel_exec 78ms, kv_fetch 140ms (miss), network_delay 24ms => total 260ms. so you see kv_fetch dominated.

[13:00] Maya Singh: that matches our logs where some requests show a big middle chunk.

[13:10] Ava Martinez: recommended mitigations summary so far: 1) improve kv hit rate by normalizing prefixes and warming; 2) cap max_wait for critical routes or route to low-latency pools; 3) profile quant kernels and enable selective fallback; 4) reduce network hops or request firewall exceptions; 5) instrument traces and correlate.

[13:40] Devin Chu: for the routing and low-latency pools — cost delta ballpark?

[13:46] Ava Martinez: typically 15-30% more per token for a dedicated low-latency pool depending on utilization — because you forgo some batching. we'll provide a pricing sheet but expect higher unit cost for 99.9SLO guarantee.

[14:05] Carlos Reyes: acceptable if it fixes p99. we care more about user experience than a small cost bump.

[14:15] Samir Patel: about the adaptive batching — we can also implement a dual-path where 5% of traffic is routed to warm nodes with prewarmed cache and minimal batching to act as canaries. that helps surface regressions quickly.

[14:34] Maya Singh: what's the onboarding time to Dedicated / low-latency pools?

[14:40] Ava Martinez: if you already have a Dedicated contract it's a config flip and some capacity prep: 1-2 weeks depending on region and GPU availability. Private on-prem deployment is longer (4-8 weeks) because of network and security setups.

[14:58] Devin Chu: we might start with a Dedicated pilot. what telemetry will you need?

[15:05] Samir Patel: sample logs (token-level), GPU perf counters, cache hit ratios, request histograms, and network captures around p99 times. we'll provide an instrumentation guide.

[15:20] Ava Martinez: we'll attach the SOC2 / compliance doc and VPC peering checklist after call.

[15:28] [16:00] brief mention of a shared doc link: /redwood/security/soc2.pdf

[15:40] Carlos Reyes: one more: we use long-context mode for some threads (8k tokens). how does that affect p99?

[15:48] Samir Patel: long contexts increase KV size and memory pressure, which raises the chance of spill and host-GPU transfers. those transfers are high variance contributors to p99. mitigation: shard long-context workloads to dedicated nodes or use prefix truncation for non-critical parts.

[16:12] Devin Chu: do you support partial KV persistence across restarts to avoid cold cache?

[16:18] Samir Patel: yes — we have a cache warmup feature to snapshot and restore hot prefixes during rolling restarts for Dedicated. that'll reduce cold-start misses.

[16:35] Maya Singh: good. please add that as a recommended config for our rollout.

[16:42] Ava Martinez: noted.

[17:12] Samir Patel: quick demo idea — we'll run a short live micro-benchmark comparing streaming vs non-streaming with KV warm and cold. caveat: this is noisy in a meeting, but should be illustrative.

[17:30] Devin Chu: okay let's do it.

[17:35] [17:35] Samir runs a micro-benchmark (paraphrased)

[18:00] Samir Patel: results (demo rough): streaming + warm KV: p50 80ms p95 210ms p99 320ms; streaming + cold KV: p50 120ms p95 380ms p99 740ms; non-streaming + warm KV: p50 140ms p95 300ms p99 420ms. so you can see cold KV massively degrades p99, streaming helps TTF but cold KV still causes big tails.

[18:40] Carlos Reyes: that's stark — explains prod behavior.

[18:50] Ava Martinez: action: run larger 1k request tests across your traffic shapes and we'll correlate after.

[19:00] discussion about mitigation sequencing and prioritized list

[19:40] Maya Singh: we want to prioritize: 1) firewall peering exceptions, 2) KV warming, 3) routing critical flows to low-latency pools, 4) quant kernel tuning.

[19:56] Samir Patel: good ordering. firewall peering may require security approvals but it's high ROI. KV warming is low-friction.

[20:10] Devin Chu: what about observability retention? we want 30 days of histograms for audits.

[20:16] Ava Martinez: retention is configurable; longer retention is an add-on. we'll send details in the pricing doc.

[20:28] Carlos Reyes: any pitfalls we should watch for during pryout?

[20:33] Samir Patel: yes: 1) don't over-quantize early, 2) watch for tail regressions after any kernel or compiler update, 3) ensure warmup scripts run on every node restart, 4) keep small % of traffic as canaries.

[20:55] Ava Martinez: ok wrapping up — recap of immediate next steps: samir runs the 1k benchmarks, devin shares prompts, maya shares network topology, ava sends docs & pricing. we'll reconvene after results.
